subject: Physics
question_text: A body is said to be in motion if it:
options_json: ["Is at rest","Changes position with time","Remains in the same position","Has constant velocity"]
explanation: Motion in physics is defined relative to a fixed reference point: a body is in motion if its position, measured from that reference point, changes as time passes. A body that is at rest or stays in the same position (A and C) is by definition not in motion, and while having a constant velocity (D) describes a specific *type* of motion, it isn't the general defining condition for motion itself — a body moving with changing velocity is still in motion too.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The SI unit of pressure is:
explanation: Pressure is defined as force per unit area (P = F/A), and its SI unit, the pascal (Pa), is equivalent to one newton of force spread over one square metre (1 Pa = 1 N/m²). The newton (A) is the unit of force itself, not pressure; the joule (C) measures energy/work; and the watt (D) measures power — each of these is a related but distinct physical quantity.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
explanation: A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction, and force clearly requires both — a push of 10 N means very different things depending on which direction it's applied. Speed, temperature, and time, by contrast, are all scalar quantities: they're fully described by a single numerical magnitude alone, with no associated direction (note that speed differs from velocity in exactly this way — velocity is the vector, speed is its scalar magnitude).
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: If two forces of 5 N and 12 N act at right angles to each other, the resultant force is:
explanation: When two forces act perpendicular to each other, their combined (resultant) effect is found using Pythagoras' theorem, since the two forces and their resultant form a right-angled triangle: resultant = √(5² + 12²) = √(25+144) = √169 = 13 N. This particular 5-12-13 combination is a well-known "Pythagorean triple," which is exactly why examiners like to use it — it gives a clean whole-number answer.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m/s in 5 seconds. What is its acceleration?
explanation: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity over time: a = (v − u) ÷ t, where v is final velocity, u is initial velocity, and t is the time taken. Here, starting from rest means u = 0, so a = (20 − 0) ÷ 5 = 4 m/s². This straightforward formula is one of the most frequently tested equations in kinematics, so it's worth having memorised cold.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The area under a velocity-time graph represents:
explanation: On a velocity-time graph, the vertical axis shows velocity and the horizontal axis shows time; multiplying velocity by time gives distance (since distance = speed × time), which geometrically corresponds exactly to the area enclosed under the graph's curve or line. This is why calculating displacement/distance from a v-t graph always involves finding the area beneath it, whether the shape is a simple rectangle, triangle, or a more complex combination.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: A machine has an efficiency of 80%. If the input work is 200 J, the output work is:
explanation: Efficiency describes what fraction of the input energy or work is successfully converted into useful output, expressed as a percentage: output = input × efficiency. Here, output = 200 J × 0.80 = 160 J — the remaining 40 J (20%) is lost, typically as heat due to friction or other inefficiencies within the machine, which is why no real machine can ever reach 100% efficiency.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: Which of the following is a good conductor of heat?
explanation: Metals like copper are excellent heat conductors because they contain a "sea" of free, mobile electrons that can rapidly transfer thermal energy through the material by colliding with each other and with the metal ions. Glass, plastic, and wood, by contrast, are all poor conductors (good insulators) of heat, because they lack this pool of free electrons and rely instead on much slower molecular vibration to pass heat along.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The amount of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C is called:
explanation: This is the precise definition of specific heat capacity — note the word "specific," meaning per unit mass (per kg), which distinguishes it from ordinary heat capacity (the heat needed to raise the temperature of a given *object*, regardless of its mass, by 1°C). Latent heat is a different concept entirely, referring to the heat absorbed or released during a change of state (melting/boiling) without any temperature change at all.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The bending of light as it passes from one medium to another is called:
explanation: Refraction occurs because light travels at different speeds in different media (e.g. faster in air than in glass or water); when light crosses the boundary between two such media at an angle, this speed change causes the light ray to bend. Reflection instead describes light bouncing back off a surface without entering the new medium at all, while dispersion is the specific splitting of white light into its component colours due to each wavelength refracting by a slightly different amount.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: When a sound wave travels from water to air, the wave property that does NOT change is:
explanation: A wave's frequency is set by whatever is generating it (the source), so as long as the source itself doesn't change, the frequency stays constant no matter what medium the wave subsequently travels through. Speed and wavelength, however, are both properties of the *medium* the wave is moving through, so as sound passes from water into air (where it travels much slower), both its speed and wavelength change noticeably, even though the frequency remains fixed.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The law of conservation of energy states that:
option_a: Energy changes from one form to another only
option_c: Energy can be created and destroyed
option_d: The total energy in an isolated system remains constant
options_json: ["Energy changes from one form to another only","Kinetic energy is always conserved","Energy can be created and destroyed","The total energy in an isolated system remains constant"]
answer_text: The total energy in an isolated system remains constant
explanation: This law states that within a closed, isolated system, the total amount of energy present never increases or decreases — it can only be transformed from one form to another (e.g. potential to kinetic, or chemical to heat), never created or destroyed outright. Option A gets close but misses the key word "total…remains constant"; option C directly contradicts the law, and option B is false in general, since kinetic energy alone often converts into other forms (like heat via friction) and isn't separately conserved.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: At resonance, the phase angle in an AC circuit is:
explanation: At the resonant frequency of a series RLC circuit, the inductive reactance and capacitive reactance exactly cancel each other out, leaving only pure resistance in the circuit. Since resistance causes no phase shift between voltage and current, the two waveforms rise and fall perfectly together at resonance — meaning the phase angle between them is exactly 0°, unlike at other frequencies where inductive or capacitive effects cause current to lead or lag voltage.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: Lenz's law works based on the principle of:
options_json: ["Conservation of momentum","Conservation of energy","Electric current","Electric charge"]
explanation: Lenz's law states that an induced current always flows in a direction that opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it. This "opposing" behaviour isn't arbitrary — if the induced current instead reinforced the change, it would create energy from nothing (a violation of energy conservation), since the system would accelerate itself indefinitely. Lenz's law is therefore really just conservation of energy applied to electromagnetic induction.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: A conductor of length 2 m carries a current of 0.8 A in a magnetic flux density of 0.5 T. The maximum force acting on it is:
explanation: The force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field is given by F = BIL, where B is flux density, I is current, and L is the conductor's length within the field. Substituting the values: F = 0.5 T × 0.8 A × 2 m = 0.8 N. This maximum value occurs when the conductor is oriented perpendicular to the magnetic field, which is the assumption implied by "maximum force" in the question.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: Power generation stations transmit electricity at very high voltage and low current to substations to reduce:
explanation: Power lost as heat in transmission cables follows the formula P(loss) = I²R — notice that this loss depends on the *square* of the current, so even a small reduction in current dramatically cuts the resulting power loss, while a change in voltage alone doesn't directly appear in that formula. By stepping voltage up (and current correspondingly down, since power = voltage × current stays roughly constant) before long-distance transmission, and then stepping voltage back down at substations, the grid minimises wasted energy over the long cable runs.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: Which of the following is a secondary colour of light?
explanation: Red, green, and blue are the three primary colours of light — they can't be made by mixing other colours together, but combining any two of them in equal amounts produces a secondary colour of light: red+blue gives magenta, red+green gives yellow, and blue+green gives cyan. This is the additive colour model used in screens and light mixing, distinct from the subtractive (pigment/paint) colour model taught for mixing paints.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: Insulators cannot conduct electricity because:
option_c: Their conduction band overlaps the valence band
options_json: ["They have no free electrons","They have many free electrons","Their conduction band overlaps the valence band","Their atoms are very large"]
explanation: Electrical conduction in a material depends on having charge carriers (usually electrons) that are free to move throughout the material under an applied voltage. In insulators, all the electrons are tightly bound within their atoms' outer shells with no free, mobile electrons available to carry current, which is exactly the opposite situation from conductors like metals, where a "sea" of loosely bound free electrons moves easily through the material.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: When a pure semiconductor is heated, its resistance:
explanation: intrinsic semiconductor resistance varies with temperature because heating creates more electron–hole pairs, changing carrier concentration and conductivity. When a pure semiconductor is heated, thermal energy excites electrons from the valence band into the conduction band, producing additional free charge carriers (electrons and holes). Increased carrier concentration raises conductivity (σ) and thus decreases resistance R (since R ∝ 1/σ), so the correct answer is 'Decreases.'\n\nThis behaviour is the negative temperature coefficient of resistance for semiconductors and is the opposite of metallic conductors, whose resistance typically increases with temperature due to enhanced lattice scattering. The option 'First increases then decreases' is misleading for a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor over ordinary temperature ranges because carrier generation dominates; only special cases or very wide temperature ranges can produce more complex curves. 'Remains the same' is inconsistent with intrinsic semiconductor physics (except for hypothetical temperature-independent resistors or superconductors, which are not described here), so it is not correct.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The thermometric substance most suitable for a very cold region is:
explanation: a thermometric substance must remain in the measurable phase and show predictable thermal expansion over the temperature range, so freezing point and linearity of expansion are key criteria. Alcohol (typically ethanol or similar organics) remains liquid to very low temperatures (ethanol ≈ −114°C) and exhibits measurable, repeatable expansion, so it functions in very cold regions. Mercury solidifies at about −39°C, so a mercury thermometer would freeze and stop working in sufficiently cold climates.\n\nWater freezes at 0°C and also shows anomalous volume behaviour near 4°C, making it unsuitable for low-temperature thermometry. Gas thermometers can operate over wide ranges without a liquid freezing, but they are bulky, require precise pressure/volume control and certain gases will condense at very low temperatures, so they are not the practical choice implied here. Therefore, of the listed options, alcohol is the most suitable practical thermometric substance for very cold regions.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The mixture of red light and cyan light produces:
explanation: Cyan light is itself already a mixture of green and blue light (a secondary colour, as in Q25). Adding red light to cyan therefore combines all three primary colours of light together — red, green, and blue — and when all three primaries are mixed in the right proportions, the result is white light, following the additive colour mixing model used for light (as opposed to pigments/paint, which mix subtractively).
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: Why does an airplane flying at high altitude produce very little sound on the ground?
option_a: Sound travels faster at high altitude
option_b: The density of air decreases at high altitude, reducing sound transmission
option_c: Sound is absorbed by the wings
option_d: The airplane is moving too fast for sound to reach the ground
options_json: ["Sound travels faster at high altitude","The density of air decreases at high altitude, reducing sound transmission","Sound is absorbed by the wings","The airplane is moving too fast for sound to reach the ground"]
answer_text: The density of air decreases at high altitude, reducing sound transmission
explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave that relies on molecules colliding with each other to transmit vibrations; at high altitude, air is much less dense (fewer air molecules per unit volume), which weakens sound transmission and causes the sound intensity reaching the ground to drop off significantly over that long vertical distance. This is distinct from the speed of sound, which actually tends to *decrease* slightly at high altitude due to lower temperature, not increase as option A incorrectly suggests.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The ebonite rod rubbed with fur acquires:
explanation: When ebonite (a hard rubber material) is rubbed with fur, electrons transfer from the fur onto the ebonite rod, leaving the rod with an excess of electrons and therefore a net negative charge, while the fur is left correspondingly positively charged (having lost electrons). This is one of the classic standard demonstrations of charging by friction used to introduce static electricity, alongside the glass-rod-and-silk pairing (which charges positively instead).
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The coefficient of friction between two perfectly smooth surfaces is:
explanation: The coefficient of friction is a numerical measure of how much resistance to sliding exists between two surfaces in contact, arising from microscopic surface roughness and interlocking irregularities. If two surfaces are truly "perfectly smooth" (an idealised, frictionless scenario), there is no roughness left to generate any resistance to sliding at all, so the coefficient of friction between them is exactly zero — this is a theoretical limiting case, since real surfaces always have at least some microscopic texture.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: A reaction will occur spontaneously when the Gibbs free energy (ΔG) is:
explanation: Gibbs free energy combines a reaction's enthalpy and entropy changes into a single value that predicts spontaneity: a negative ΔG means the process releases usable free energy and will proceed spontaneously without needing outside energy input. A positive ΔG means the reverse process is spontaneous instead (the forward reaction would need energy input to occur), and ΔG = 0 marks a system exactly at equilibrium, neither favouring forward nor reverse.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: In optical fibre deployment, the principle applied is:
explanation: Optical fibres carry light signals over long distances by having light strike the boundary between the fibre's core and its outer cladding at an angle greater than the critical angle, causing it to reflect entirely back into the core instead of escaping — total internal reflection. This allows the light signal to bounce along the length of the fibre with minimal loss, repeatedly reflecting internally rather than refracting out through the sides.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The molecular nature of matter is NOT supported by:
explanation: Brownian motion (the random jittering of visible particles caused by invisible molecular collisions), diffusion (particles spreading due to random molecular movement), and surface tension (a result of unbalanced intermolecular attractive forces at a liquid's surface) all provide direct experimental evidence that matter consists of moving, interacting molecules. Reflection, by contrast, is simply a bulk optical phenomenon describing how light bounces off a surface, and doesn't itself reveal anything about the underlying molecular structure of the reflecting material.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The lightning conductor works by the principle of electrostatic:
explanation: Sharp, pointed conductors concentrate electric charge much more intensely at their tip than a flat or rounded surface would, because charge density increases dramatically at points of small radius of curvature. This intense charge concentration ionises the surrounding air, allowing accumulated atmospheric charge to leak away gradually and quietly (as a corona discharge) through the lightning conductor's point, rather than building up to the point of triggering a dangerous direct lightning strike on the building.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: In a compound microscope, the eyepiece focal length is:
explanation: A compound microscope achieves its high magnification by using two converging lenses, both with comparatively short focal lengths — this is what distinguishes a microscope's optical design from a telescope, which instead uses a long-focal-length objective lens. While the objective lens typically has an even shorter focal length than the eyepiece (to achieve strong initial magnification of the tiny specimen), both lenses in a microscope are "short" focal length lenses relative to telescope design.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: Calculate the normal reaction on a 10 kg body in an elevator accelerating upward at 5 m/s². [g = 10 m/s²]
explanation: When an elevator accelerates upward, the normal reaction force from the floor must be greater than the body's ordinary weight, because it needs to both support the weight *and* provide the extra force needed to accelerate the body upward: N − mg = ma, so N = m(g+a). Substituting the values: N = 10 × (10+5) = 150 N — notice that if the elevator were instead accelerating downward, the normal reaction would be correspondingly *less* than the body's weight.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The EMF induced in the secondary winding of a transformer is:
explanation: Transformers operate exclusively on alternating current, because only a continuously *changing* current in the primary coil produces the changing magnetic flux needed to induce an EMF in the secondary coil (per Faraday's law). Since the primary current is itself constantly alternating, the magnetic flux it produces is also constantly changing, and so the induced EMF in the secondary winding correspondingly varies (alternates) in step with it, rather than settling to any fixed steady value.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: What is the primary function of a fuse in an electric circuit?
options_json: ["To increase voltage","To decrease resistance","To protect against overcurrent","To filter out AC"]
explanation:
A fuse provides overcurrent protection by containing a thin metal link that melts when current exceeds a rated value, thereby opening the circuit.
When excessive current flows from a fault or short circuit the fuse element heats and melts faster than other components, isolating and protecting wiring and appliances from overheating or fire.
It does not increase voltage — voltage is set by sources or transformers, not by a passive safety device like a fuse.
Fuses are specified by current rating and breaking capacity and must be replaced with the correct type and rating, because using a higher-rated fuse or bypassing it defeats the intended overcurrent protection.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: If a cell has EMF of 2.6 V and internal resistance of 0.2 Ω connected to a 3.5 Ω resistor, what is the current?
explanation: A real cell's internal resistance acts in series with any external circuit resistance, so the total resistance the current must flow through is the external resistor plus the internal resistance combined: I = EMF ÷ (R + r) = 2.6 ÷ (3.5 + 0.2) = 2.6 ÷ 3.7 ≈ 0.70 A. This is why a cell's terminal voltage (what you'd measure across its terminals) is always slightly less than its EMF whenever current is flowing — some voltage is "lost" driving current through the cell's own internal resistance.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: Three capacitors: 2 μF and 4 μF in parallel, then in series with 3 μF. Effective capacitance is:
explanation: Capacitors in parallel simply add together (unlike resistors), so the 2 μF and 4 μF pair combines to 2+4 = 6 μF. This combined 6 μF then sits in series with the remaining 3 μF capacitor, and series capacitors combine using the reciprocal formula: 1/C = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6 = 1/2, giving C = 2 μF. Remember that capacitor combination rules are the *opposite* of resistor combination rules — parallel adds directly, series uses reciprocals.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: An object is projected horizontally from a height of 50 cm. How long does it take to reach the ground? [g = 10 m/s²]
explanation: For horizontal projectile motion, the time to fall depends only on the vertical drop height, completely independent of how fast the object is moving horizontally — this is because gravity only acts vertically. Using h = ½gt² with h = 0.5 m (converting 50 cm to metres first): 0.5 = ½ × 10 × t², giving t² = 0.1, so t = √0.1 ≈ 0.32 s.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: Convert 102°F to °C:
explanation:
Use the Fahrenheit–to–Celsius conversion formula: °C = (°F − 32) × 5/9.
Substitute 102°F: (102 − 32) = 70, so °C = 70 × 5/9 = 350/9 °C.
350/9 = 38.888… which rounds to 38.9°C, matching the correct option.
The exact value 350/9 °C rounded to one decimal place is 38.9°C, so option '38.9°C' is the correct choice.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: As the temperature of a liquid increases, its surface tension:
explanation: Surface tension arises from the cohesive attractive forces between molecules at a liquid's surface pulling inward. As temperature rises, molecules gain more kinetic energy and move around more vigorously, which weakens the effectiveness of these cohesive intermolecular attractions, so the surface tension of the liquid decreases as it gets hotter — this is why warm water, for example, "wets" surfaces and forms lather more easily than cold water.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: Which energy source does NOT use a turbine in electricity generation?
explanation:
Photovoltaic (PV) solar generation relies on the photovoltaic effect, where semiconductor junctions convert photons directly into electric current without moving parts.
Because PV cells produce electrical energy directly, no mechanical shaft, turbine or generator is required, so 'Solar (photovoltaic)' is the correct choice.
Nuclear power uses heat from fission to make high-pressure steam that spins steam turbines coupled to electrical generators.
Be careful: concentrated solar thermal (CSP) systems use mirrors to produce steam and do use turbines, so the question's use of 'photovoltaic' specifically distinguishes it from turbine-using solar technologies.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The dispersion of white light is:
option_a: The speed increase of white light in a prism
option_b: The separation of white light into its component colours
option_c: The reflection of light off a prism surface
options_json: ["The speed increase of white light in a prism","The separation of white light into its component colours","The reflection of light off a prism surface","The absorption of UV light"]
answer_text: The separation of white light into its component colours
explanation: White light is actually a mixture of many different wavelengths (colours) of visible light all travelling together. When it passes through a prism, each wavelength refracts by a slightly different amount (since refractive index varies slightly with wavelength), causing the different colours to separate out and spread into a visible spectrum — this separation process is what's meant by dispersion, and it's the effect responsible for both prism spectra and natural rainbows.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: If the wavelength of a wave is 3 cm, the wave number is:
explanation:
Wavenumber is defined as the reciprocal of the wavelength: wavenumber = 1/λ, with units of inverse length (e.g. cm⁻¹).
Substituting λ = 3 cm gives wavenumber = 1/3 cm⁻¹ = 0.333… cm⁻¹, normally reported as 0.33 cm⁻¹.
Therefore option B (0.33 cm⁻¹) is the correct numerical value for the given wavelength.
Wavenumber should not be confused with frequency (Hz); they are related by f = v/λ where v is wave speed, so frequency has s⁻¹ units while wavenumber has cm⁻¹.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: Phosphorus has a decay constant of 5.85 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Its half-life is:
explanation: radioactive decay constant λ and half-life t½ are related by t½ = ln2/λ, where ln2 ≈ 0.693. Substituting λ = 5.85 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ gives t½ = 0.693 ÷ 5.85×10⁻³ ≈ 118.5 s. Therefore the correct option is 118.5 s because it is the direct result of that calculation.\n\nThe 170.9 s choice equals the mean lifetime τ = 1/λ ≈ 170.94 s, which is often confused with half-life but is a different quantity. The option 5.85 × 10⁻³ s is just the decay constant value (with units s⁻¹), not a time interval, so it cannot be the half-life. 5.0 s is far too small and would arise from a numerical or formula error rather than the correct ln2/λ relation.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: A ball is dropped from 50 m. Time to reach the ground is: [g = 10 m/s²]
explanation: Using the free-fall equation h = ½gt² with h = 50 m: 50 = ½ × 10 × t², so 50 = 5t², giving t² = 10, and therefore t = √10 ≈ 3.16 s. The answer is deliberately left in surd form (√10 s) as one of the options, which is a useful reminder that JAMB-style answers sometimes prefer exact irrational forms over rounded decimals — always check whether an option like this is hiding among the choices before assuming you've made an arithmetic error.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: A 10 kg block is lifted vertically upwards by 2 m. What is the work done? [g = 10 m/s²]
explanation: Work done against gravity when lifting an object is calculated as W = mgh, where m is mass, g is the acceleration due to gravity, and h is the height risen. Substituting the given values: W = 10 kg × 10 m/s² × 2 m = 200 J. Note that this question uses g = 10 m/s² (the rounded value), which is why the answer isn't 196 J (that would use g = 9.8 m/s² instead) — always use whichever value of g the question explicitly provides.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: A metre rule is pivoted at its midpoint. A 120 N force hangs 25 cm from the pivot. Where must a 20 N force hang to balance it?
explanation: For a rule balanced at its pivot, the principle of moments requires the clockwise and anticlockwise turning effects to be equal: (force) × (distance from pivot) must match on both sides. Setting the two moments equal: 120 N × 25 cm = 20 N × d, so d = (120×25) ÷ 20 = 3000 ÷ 20 = 150 cm — note that the required distance exceeds the length of a standard metre rule's arm from the centre, illustrating why the smaller force needs to be placed proportionally much further out to balance the larger one.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: What is the principle behind the operation of a transformer?
explanation: A transformer works by passing an alternating current through a primary coil, which creates a constantly changing magnetic field. This changing field induces a corresponding alternating EMF in a nearby secondary coil — a direct application of Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction, which states that a changing magnetic flux through a coil induces an EMF in it. Without a *changing* current (as in DC), no such induction would occur, which is why transformers only work with AC.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: A car travels 200 km in 4 hours. What is its average speed?
explanation:
Average speed is defined as total distance travelled divided by total time taken: v_avg = d/t.
Applying this to the question gives v_avg = 200 km ÷ 4 h = 50 km/h.
Therefore the correct option is 50 km/h because it equals the straightforward distance-over-time calculation.
75 km/h is also wrong and would result from an arithmetic mistake or an incorrect averaging of different speeds, not from d/t with the given data.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: What is the term for the opposition to the flow of electric current?
explanation: Resistance is defined precisely as the opposition a material offers to the flow of electric current, measured in ohms; the higher a component's resistance, the more it restricts current flow for a given voltage (following Ohm's law, V = IR). Conductance is actually the reciprocal of resistance (how easily current flows), while inductance and capacitance describe entirely different circuit properties related to changing currents and stored charge respectively.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: Which instrument is most suitable for measuring the diameter of a thin wire?
explanation: A screw gauge (micrometer) can measure to a precision of about 0.01 mm, using a fine calibrated screw thread to close in on the object being measured — far more precise than a metre rule or tape measure, which are only marked in millimetres and are too coarse for something as thin as a wire. A vernier calliper improves on the ruler's precision (to about 0.01–0.02 cm) but is still less precise than a screw gauge for very small, thin objects like wire diameters.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part1.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: Which property of a wave determines its energy?
explanation: For a mechanical wave (such as a wave on a string or a sound wave), the energy it carries is proportional to the square of its amplitude — a wave with twice the amplitude carries four times the energy. This is why, for example, a louder sound (larger amplitude) delivers noticeably more energy to your eardrum than a quieter one of the same frequency, even though both waves might travel at the same speed and have the same wavelength.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: Instrument for measuring relative humidity:
explanation: A hygrometer is specifically designed to measure the amount of water vapour present in the air relative to the maximum it could hold at that temperature (relative humidity). This is distinct from a barometer (measures atmospheric pressure), a hydrometer (measures the density/specific gravity of liquids), and a thermometer (measures temperature) — the similar-sounding names of these instruments make them a common source of confusion in exams, so it's worth deliberately memorising each one's specific purpose.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The SI unit of power is:
explanation: Power is defined as the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred, i.e. energy divided by time, and its SI unit, the watt, is equivalent to one joule of energy transferred per second (1 W = 1 J/s). The joule (A) measures energy/work itself, without any reference to time, while newton (B) measures force and pascal (D) measures pressure — each a related but separate quantity from power.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: At resonance in a series RLC AC circuit:
option_c: Impedance equals resistance and current is maximum
options_json: ["Impedance is maximum","Current is minimum","Impedance equals resistance and current is maximum","Capacitive reactance exceeds inductive reactance"]
answer_text: Impedance equals resistance and current is maximum
explanation: At the resonant frequency, the inductive reactance and capacitive reactance in a series RLC circuit become exactly equal in magnitude and cancel each other out entirely, leaving total impedance equal to just the resistance, R (its minimum possible value). Since current is inversely related to impedance for a fixed voltage (I = V/Z), this minimum impedance corresponds to the maximum possible current flowing in the circuit — the opposite of what options A and B claim.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The working principle of a simple electric motor is based on:
options_json: ["Magnetic effect of current","Chemical effect of current","Heating effect of current","Electrostatic induction"]
explanation: An electric motor works because a current-carrying coil placed within a magnetic field experiences a force (following the motor effect, related to F = BIL), and this force causes the coil to rotate continuously as its current direction is periodically reversed by a commutator. This is fundamentally different from the chemical effect (used in electrolysis/batteries) or heating effect (used in heaters/fuses) of current — a motor's operation depends specifically on the magnetic force current-carrying conductors experience in a magnetic field.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: A transformer has 200 turns in the primary and 1000 turns in the secondary. If the primary voltage is 50 V, the secondary voltage is:
explanation: The transformer equation relates voltage to the ratio of turns on each coil: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np. Rearranging and substituting: Vs = Vp × (Ns/Np) = 50 × (1000/200) = 50 × 5 = 250 V. Because the secondary coil has more turns than the primary (a "step-up" transformer), the output voltage is correspondingly higher than the input voltage — the opposite arrangement (fewer secondary turns) would instead step voltage down.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The energy stored in a stretched spring is called:
options_json: ["Kinetic energy","Gravitational potential energy","Elastic potential energy","Chemical energy"]
explanation: When a spring is stretched or compressed from its natural length, work is done against its internal restoring forces, and this work is stored within the spring as elastic potential energy, ready to be released and converted into kinetic energy once the spring is allowed to return toward its natural shape. This differs from gravitational potential energy (stored due to height in a gravitational field) and kinetic energy (energy of motion), even though all three are related forms of mechanical energy that commonly interconvert in oscillating spring systems.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: Newton's second law of motion states that the rate of change of momentum is:
options_json: ["Inversely proportional to force","Equal to the applied force","Equal to acceleration","Proportional to mass only"]
explanation: Newton's second law can be expressed precisely as F = Δp/Δt (force equals the rate of change of momentum), which for a constant mass simplifies to the more familiar F = ma. This makes force directly (not inversely) proportional to the rate of momentum change, and the relationship holds even in cases where mass itself is changing (such as a rocket losing fuel mass), which the simpler F = ma version can't fully capture on its own.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The pitch of a sound wave is determined by its:
explanation: Pitch is our subjective perception of how "high" or "low" a sound is, and it corresponds directly to the sound wave's frequency: higher frequency waves are perceived as higher-pitched sounds, and lower frequency waves as lower-pitched. Amplitude, by contrast, determines loudness (volume) rather than pitch — a common point of confusion, since both are properties of the same wave but affect completely different aspects of how we perceive the sound.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: Which of the following correctly states Boyle's law?
options_json: ["V ∝ T at constant P","P ∝ T at constant V","PV = constant at constant T","P/T = constant at constant V"]
explanation: Boyle's law specifically describes an inverse relationship between pressure and volume for a fixed mass of gas held at constant temperature, mathematically expressed as PV = constant (or equivalently P₁V₁ = P₂V₂). Options A and B actually describe Charles' law and Gay-Lussac's (Pressure) law respectively — matching the correct named law to its correct pair of variables (and which one is held fixed) is exactly what this question is testing.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The Doppler effect is the change in observed frequency when:
option_a: A wave source and observer move relative to each other
option_b: A wave passes through two slits
option_d: Sound reflects off a hard surface
options_json: ["A wave source and observer move relative to each other","A wave passes through two slits","Light bends around an obstacle","Sound reflects off a hard surface"]
answer_text: A wave source and observer move relative to each other
explanation: The Doppler effect describes how the observed frequency of a wave shifts higher when the source and observer are moving closer together, and shifts lower when they're moving further apart — this is why a passing ambulance siren sounds higher-pitched as it approaches and lower-pitched as it moves away. Options B, C, and D instead describe entirely different wave phenomena (interference/diffraction, diffraction, and reflection respectively), unrelated to relative motion between source and observer.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: A body of mass 5 kg falls from a height of 10 m. What is its kinetic energy just before hitting the ground? [g = 10 m/s²]
explanation: By the principle of conservation of energy (ignoring air resistance), all of the gravitational potential energy the body had at the top of its fall converts entirely into kinetic energy by the time it reaches the ground: KE = PE(lost) = mgh = 5 kg × 10 m/s² × 10 m = 500 J. This is a useful shortcut — you don't need to separately calculate the falling velocity first and then apply ½mv², since energy conservation lets you jump straight from height to final kinetic energy.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: Which of the following is an example of rectilinear (straight-line) motion?
option_b: Motion of a planet around the sun
option_c: A stone dropped vertically from rest
option_d: Motion of a car around a bend
options_json: ["Motion of a pendulum","Motion of a planet around the sun","A stone dropped vertically from rest","Motion of a car around a bend"]
answer_text: A stone dropped vertically from rest
explanation: Rectilinear motion specifically means motion along a straight-line path, and a stone dropped straight down from rest falls in exactly a vertical straight line under gravity, with no sideways component to its path. A pendulum swings along a curved arc, a planet follows a roughly elliptical orbital path, and a car turning a bend follows a curved road — all three of these involve curved, not straight-line, motion.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The image formed by a plane mirror is:
options_json: ["Real, inverted, same size","Virtual, erect, same size","Real, erect, magnified","Virtual, inverted, diminished"]
explanation: A plane (flat) mirror always forms a virtual image — meaning light rays only *appear* to come from behind the mirror, rather than actually converging there — that is upright (erect, not inverted) and exactly the same size as the original object, with the image appearing as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it. This is the simplest and most predictable of all mirror image types, unlike curved mirrors, whose image properties depend on the object's distance from the mirror.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: When an object is placed at the focus of a concave mirror, the image formed is:
options_json: ["At infinity","At the centre of curvature","Between F and the mirror","Behind the mirror"]
explanation: When an object sits exactly at a concave mirror's principal focus, the reflected rays that were converging toward or diverging from that point instead emerge from the mirror perfectly parallel to each other after reflection, never actually meeting to form a real image at any finite distance. Since parallel rays are mathematically treated as meeting "at infinity," this is the standard way of describing this special-case image location.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The critical angle for a medium is the angle of incidence in the denser medium at which the angle of refraction is:
explanation: The critical angle is defined as the specific angle of incidence (measured in the denser medium) at which the refracted ray no longer bends into the less dense medium at a normal angle, but instead travels exactly along the boundary surface itself — meaning the angle of refraction has reached 90°. Any angle of incidence beyond this critical angle results in total internal reflection instead of refraction, which is the principle underlying optical fibres (Q34).
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: Charles' law states that at constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is:
option_c: Proportional to the square of temperature
options_json: ["Inversely proportional to temperature","Directly proportional to absolute temperature","Proportional to the square of temperature","Independent of temperature"]
explanation: Charles' law describes a direct proportionality between the volume of a fixed mass of gas and its absolute (Kelvin) temperature, provided pressure is kept constant: V ∝ T, or equivalently V/T = constant. This means that as a gas is heated at constant pressure, it expands proportionally, and cooled gas contracts proportionally — note that this direct relationship only holds when temperature is measured in Kelvin, not Celsius or Fahrenheit.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: A projectile is launched horizontally. The vertical component of its velocity after time t is:
explanation: In horizontal projectile motion, gravity acts only in the vertical direction, continuously accelerating the object downward from an initial vertical velocity of zero. Using v = u + at with u = 0 vertically, the vertical velocity after time t simply becomes v = gt, growing steadily as the object falls — meanwhile, the horizontal velocity component stays completely unaffected by gravity and remains constant throughout the entire flight, since no horizontal force acts on the projectile.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: An electric iron is rated 1000 W, 240 V. What is the current it draws?
explanation: Electrical power is related to voltage and current by P = VI, so current can be found by rearranging: I = P/V = 1000 ÷ 240 ≈ 4.17 A. This kind of "rated power and voltage → find current" calculation is extremely common in practical electricity questions, since it's exactly the sort of figure you'd need to know to select an appropriately rated fuse for a real household appliance.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The phenomenon of light bending around the edges of an obstacle is called:
explanation: Diffraction occurs when a wave encounters an obstacle or narrow gap comparable in size to its own wavelength, causing the wave to spread out and bend around the edges of that obstacle rather than travelling in a strictly straight line past it. This is distinct from refraction, which involves bending due to a *change of medium* (and therefore speed), not bending around a physical obstacle's edge.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The unit of radioactivity (rate of decay) is the:
explanation: radioactivity (activity) is the rate of nuclear disintegration expressed as the number of decay events per unit time. Becquerel (Bq) is the SI unit of activity defined as one nuclear disintegration per second, so it directly measures the decay rate and is the correct choice. Gray (Gy) measures absorbed dose — the energy deposited per kilogram of material (1 Gy = 1 J kg^-1) — and therefore describes dose, not source activity.\n\nSievert (Sv) measures dose equivalent, which weights absorbed dose for biological effect and so quantifies biological harm rather than the decay rate of the source. Roentgen (R) is an older unit of exposure that quantifies ionisation in air and is not a direct measure of the source's disintegration rate; it has largely been superseded by SI units. For scale, the historical curie (Ci) is 3.7 × 10^10 Bq, emphasising that activity is a count-rate quantity distinct from absorbed or equivalent dose.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The mass-energy equivalence formula is given by Einstein as:
explanation: This is Einstein's famous equation from special relativity, showing that mass and energy are fundamentally interchangeable — a small amount of mass corresponds to an enormous amount of energy, since c (the speed of light) is squared in the formula. The other three options are different, unrelated equations from classical mechanics: ½mv² is kinetic energy, and mgh is gravitational potential energy — neither of which describes the mass-energy equivalence Einstein proposed.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: Which of the following is NOT a longitudinal wave?
options_json: ["Sound wave in air","Ultrasound wave","Light wave","Seismic P-wave"]
explanation:
The concept is longitudinal versus transverse waves: longitudinal waves have particle oscillations parallel to the direction of propagation (compressions and rarefactions).
Mechanical waves such as sound in air, ultrasound (high‑frequency sound), and seismic P‑waves propagate by particle compression and rarefaction and are therefore longitudinal.
Light is an electromagnetic wave whose electric and magnetic fields oscillate perpendicular to the direction of travel and it does not require a material medium.
Hence 'Light wave' is NOT a longitudinal wave and is the correct answer.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The viscosity of a liquid:
option_d: First increases then decreases with temperature
options_json: ["Increases with temperature","Decreases with temperature","Is unaffected by temperature","First increases then decreases with temperature"]
explanation: Viscosity is a measure of a liquid's internal resistance to flow, arising from intermolecular attractive forces between its molecules. As temperature rises, molecules gain kinetic energy and move around more freely, which weakens the effectiveness of these intermolecular attractions and allows the liquid to flow more easily — this is why honey or engine oil becomes noticeably runnier when warmed, and thicker/more resistant to flow when cold.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: An ammeter is connected in a circuit to measure current. It should be connected:
option_d: In parallel with the power supply
options_json: ["In parallel with the component","In series with the component","Across the power supply only","In parallel with the power supply"]
explanation: An ammeter must be connected in series with the component being measured, so that the *entire* current flowing through that part of the circuit is forced to pass directly through the meter itself, allowing an accurate reading of that current. Ammeters are deliberately designed with very low internal resistance specifically so that inserting them in series barely affects the circuit's overall current — connecting one in parallel instead (as with a voltmeter) would create a short-circuit path and give a meaningless or damaging reading.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: A simple pendulum completes 20 oscillations in 40 seconds. What is its period?
explanation: The period of oscillation is the time taken for just one complete swing back and forth, found by dividing the total time by the total number of oscillations: T = 40 s ÷ 20 = 2 s. Take care not to confuse "period" (time per one oscillation) with the total time given in the question or with frequency (oscillations per second, which would instead be 20/40 = 0.5 Hz here) — these are easy to mix up under time pressure.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The boiling point of a liquid increases when:
options_json: ["Pressure is decreased","Pressure is increased","The liquid is cooled","More solvent is added"]
explanation: A liquid boils once its vapour pressure rises to match the external (atmospheric) pressure pressing down on it. If the external pressure is increased, the liquid's vapour pressure must also rise further — requiring a higher temperature — before boiling can begin, which is exactly why boiling point rises with increased pressure (the principle exploited by pressure cookers to cook food faster at higher-than-normal boiling temperatures).
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: Which of the following demonstrates the wave nature of light?
explanation: Interference (light waves overlapping to produce alternating bright and dark bands) can only be explained if light behaves as a wave, since it depends fundamentally on wave properties like phase and superposition. The photoelectric effect, Compton effect, and pair production, by contrast, are all phenomena that can only be properly explained by treating light as discrete particles (photons) — together, these contrasting phenomena illustrate light's famous wave-particle duality.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The latent heat of fusion is the heat energy required to:
option_a: Raise the temperature of a solid by 1°C
option_b: Convert a liquid to a gas at constant temperature
option_c: Convert a solid to a liquid at constant temperature
options_json: ["Raise the temperature of a solid by 1°C","Convert a liquid to a gas at constant temperature","Convert a solid to a liquid at constant temperature","Cool a gas to liquid"]
answer_text: Convert a solid to a liquid at constant temperature
explanation: Latent heat of fusion is specifically the energy absorbed when a substance changes from solid to liquid (melting) at its melting point, without any accompanying rise in temperature — the absorbed energy instead goes entirely into breaking the intermolecular bonds holding the solid's rigid structure together. This is distinct from latent heat of vaporisation (option B, which describes the liquid-to-gas transition instead) and from specific heat capacity, which involves an actual temperature change rather than a change of state.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: A moving coil galvanometer measures:
explanation: A galvanometer detects and measures very small electric currents by using the current-carrying coil's interaction with a magnetic field (the same magnetic-force principle as an electric motor) to produce a proportional deflection of a pointer or needle. With appropriate additional resistors, a galvanometer can be adapted into an ammeter (for larger currents) or a voltmeter (for voltage), but in its basic form it is fundamentally a small-current-measuring instrument.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The Archimedes principle states that the upthrust on a body immersed in a fluid is equal to:
option_b: The weight of the fluid displaced
options_json: ["The mass of the body","The weight of the fluid displaced","The volume of the body","The density of the fluid"]
answer_text: The weight of the fluid displaced
explanation: Archimedes' principle states that any object submerged (fully or partially) in a fluid experiences an upward buoyant force (upthrust) equal in magnitude to the weight of the fluid that the object has displaced — not the object's own mass, volume, or the fluid's density alone, though all of these factor indirectly into calculating that displaced fluid's weight. This principle explains why objects float when their displaced fluid's weight can support their own weight, and sink when it cannot.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: Which Newton's law explains why a gun recoils when fired?
explanation: Newton's third law states that for every action force, there is an equal and opposite reaction force. When a gun fires, it exerts a large forward force on the bullet (the action), and by Newton's third law, the bullet simultaneously exerts an equal and opposite backward force on the gun (the reaction) — this backward push is what we feel and observe as the gun's recoil.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The work function of a metal is the minimum energy required to:
option_a: Heat the metal to its melting point
option_b: Remove an electron from the surface of the metal
options_json: ["Heat the metal to its melting point","Remove an electron from the surface of the metal","Ionise the metal","Magnetise the metal"]
answer_text: Remove an electron from the surface of the metal
explanation: The work function is a key concept in the photoelectric effect: it represents the minimum amount of energy needed to free (eject) an electron from the surface of a particular metal, overcoming the attractive forces holding it in place. Only incoming light with photon energy equal to or greater than this work function can eject electrons at all, regardless of the light's intensity — light below this threshold frequency, no matter how bright, produces no photoelectric emission.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: A convex mirror always produces an image that is:
options_json: ["Real, inverted, magnified","Real, inverted, diminished","Virtual, erect, diminished","Virtual, erect, magnified"]
explanation: A convex (outward-curving) mirror always forms a virtual image behind the mirror's surface — since the reflected rays only *appear* to diverge from a point behind it — and this image is always upright (erect) and smaller than the actual object (diminished), regardless of how far away the object is placed. This predictable, always-diminished field of view is exactly why convex mirrors are used for car side mirrors and shop security mirrors, giving a wider view of the surroundings.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The half-life of a radioactive substance is the time taken for:
option_d: The substance to lose half its mass to heat
options_json: ["All the atoms to decay","Half the atoms to decay","The activity to reach zero","The substance to lose half its mass to heat"]
explanation: Half-life is defined as the time required for exactly half of the radioactive atoms in a sample to undergo decay, reducing the number of remaining undecayed nuclei to 50% of the original amount. This process continues indefinitely in successive half-lives (half of what remains decays in each subsequent equal time interval), meaning the sample's activity approaches zero only in the mathematical limit, never technically reaching absolute zero within any finite number of half-lives.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: A voltmeter reads 12 V across a resistor through which a current of 3 A flows. The resistance is:
explanation: Ohm's law relates potential difference V, current I and resistance R by the equation V = IR. Rearrange to R = V/I and substitute the given values: R = 12 V ÷ 3 A = 4 Ω. The correct option 4 Ω equals this computed resistance and uses the SI unit ohm (Ω), which is volt per ampere.\n\nOption 3 Ω would result from an arithmetic slip (for example dividing by 4 instead of 3) and does not match the given current and voltage. Option 36 Ω arises from multiplying V and I (12 × 3), a confusion of V = IR with R = V/I, while 0.25 Ω is the reciprocal of 4 Ω and reflects inverting the ratio. Always keep units V and A in the calculation so that R has units V/A = Ω and you can check your answer by verifying V = IR.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The pressure at the bottom of a liquid column of height h and density ρ is:
explanation: Pressure due to a liquid column depends on three factors multiplied together: the liquid's density (ρ), the acceleration due to gravity (g), and the height (depth) of the column (h), giving the standard formula P = ρgh. Notice this formula doesn't depend on the container's cross-sectional area or shape at all — a tall, narrow column and a tall, wide column of the same liquid and same height exert exactly the same pressure at the bottom.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The energy of a photon is given by:
explanation: A photon's energy is directly proportional to its frequency, related by Planck's constant: E = hf, where h is Planck's constant and f is the photon's frequency. This relationship is the mathematical foundation of quantum theory and the photoelectric effect (see Q82) — higher-frequency light (like ultraviolet or gamma rays) carries much more energy per photon than lower-frequency light (like radio waves or infrared), even before considering the *number* of photons (intensity) involved.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: In a series circuit, three resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω, and 5 Ω are connected. The total resistance is:
explanation: resistors connected in series share the same current and their resistances add algebraically, so R_total = ΣR. Calculate: R_total = 2 Ω + 3 Ω + 5 Ω = 10 Ω, which corresponds to the option '10 Ω'. Why addition: each resistor drops part of the total voltage while carrying the common current, so the total opposition to current is the sum of individual resistances.\n\nDistractor '1 Ω' arises from confusing series with parallel (1/R = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/5 ≈ 1.033, so R ≈ 0.97 Ω ≈ 1 Ω), showing why that choice is tempting but incorrect here. Distractor '30 Ω' looks like an incorrect multiplication (2×3×5) and '0.1 Ω' is the reciprocal of 10 Ω (a conductance error); neither follows the series rule. Application: with R_total = 10 Ω the circuit current for a supply voltage V is I = V/10 Ω by Ohm's law, illustrating the practical need to sum series resistances.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: In a parallel circuit, two resistors of 6 Ω and 3 Ω are connected. The total resistance is:
explanation: For resistors connected in parallel, the combined resistance is always *less* than the smallest individual resistor, since parallel connection provides multiple alternative paths for current to flow. Using the reciprocal formula: 1/R = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6 = 1/2, so R = 2 Ω — notice this result (2 Ω) is indeed smaller than either the 6 Ω or 3 Ω resistor individually, exactly as expected for a parallel combination.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: Which type of radioactive decay increases the atomic number by 1?
explanation: In beta-minus decay, a neutron inside the nucleus transforms into a proton, releasing a fast-moving electron (the beta particle) in the process. Since the number of protons (which determines atomic number) increases by exactly one while the mass number stays the same, this shifts the element one place to the right in the periodic table — the opposite of beta-plus decay, which instead converts a proton into a neutron, *decreasing* the atomic number by 1.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: A 500 W electric heater is used for 2 hours. The electrical energy consumed is:
explanation: Electrical energy consumed is power multiplied by time, but time must be converted into seconds to give an answer in joules: 2 hours = 2 × 3600 = 7200 seconds. Then: E = Pt = 500 W × 7200 s = 3,600,000 J. This is a common trap question, since forgetting to convert hours into seconds (or accidentally multiplying by 2 instead of 7200) leads directly to one of the incorrect distractor options.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The refractive index of glass is 1.5. What is the critical angle for glass-air interface?
explanation: The critical angle relates to refractive index by the formula sin(C) = 1/n, where n is the refractive index of the denser medium (glass, here). Substituting: sin(C) = 1/1.5 ≈ 0.667, so C = sin⁻¹(0.667) ≈ 41.8°. This calculation links directly back to Q65's definition of critical angle — recognising when to apply this specific formula (whenever refractive index is given and critical angle is asked for) is a frequently tested skill.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: Newton's first law (law of inertia) states that a body remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted upon by:
explanation: Newton's first law (the law of inertia) states that an object will continue in its current state of rest or uniform straight-line motion unless a net (resultant) external force acts to change that state. The key word is "resultant" — if multiple forces act on a body but perfectly cancel each other out, there is effectively no net force, and the body's motion remains unchanged, exactly as if no forces were acting on it at all.
source_label: Owner-provided Markdown · phys_part2.md · Physics

subject: Physics
question_text: The Principle of Moments states that for a body in equilibrium:
option_b: Sum of clockwise moments = Sum of anticlockwise moments
option_c: The centre of gravity is at the pivot
option_d: All forces act through the same point
options_json: ["Total forces are zero","Sum of clockwise moments = Sum of anticlockwise moments","The centre of gravity is at the pivot","All forces act through the same point"]
answer_text: Sum of clockwise moments = Sum of anticlockwise moments
explanation: The Principle of Moments specifically addresses rotational equilibrium: for a body to remain balanced and not rotate, the total turning effect (moment) trying to rotate it clockwise around any chosen pivot point must exactly equal the total turning effect trying to rotate it anticlockwise. question_text: [Mechanics — Simple Machines] The velocity ratio of a machine is 5 and its efficiency is 75%. What effort would be needed to lift a load of 150N with the machine?
explanation: Efficiency = Mechanical Advantage ÷ Velocity Ratio, so MA = efficiency × VR = 0.75 × 5 = 3.75. Since MA = Load/Effort, Effort = Load/MA = 150/3.75 = 40N. A common trap is using VR directly as MA (ignoring the 75% efficiency loss), which would give 30N instead — always apply efficiency before dividing for effort in a non-ideal machine.

explanation: Fresh water is less dense than salt water, so by Archimedes' principle the ship must displace a greater volume of fresh water to generate the same upward buoyant force equal to its weight. This means the ship sinks lower, decreasing the fraction of its volume that remains above the surface. This is the same principle behind Plimsoll lines marked on ship hulls for different water types.

explanation: Current in the cable: I = P/V = 3000/1500 = 2A. Power loss in the cable resistance: P_loss = I²R = 2² × 20 = 80W. This is the core reason power is transmitted at high voltage/low current over long distances — halving current quarters the resistive loss. question_text: [Solid State Physics — Semiconductors] In a pure semiconductor, the number of electrons in the conduction band is
option_a: less than the number of holes in the valence band
option_b: equal to the number of holes in the valence band
option_c: greater than the number of holes in the valence band
option_d: twice the number of holes in the valence band
options_json: ["less than the number of holes in the valence band","equal to the number of holes in the valence band","greater than the number of holes in the valence band","twice the number of holes in the valence band"]

explanation: In an intrinsic (pure, undoped) semiconductor, every electron that is thermally excited into the conduction band leaves behind exactly one hole in the valence band. Electron-hole pairs are always created and destroyed together, so their populations stay equal at all times. This equality breaks down only in doped (extrinsic) semiconductors, where impurities deliberately create an excess of one carrier type.

question_text: [Optics — Lenses / Magnification] A projection lantern is used to give the image of a slide on a screen. If the image is 24 times as large as the slide and the screen is 72.0m from the projecting lens, what is the position of the slide from the lens?
explanation: Linear magnification m = v/u, where v is image distance and u is object (slide) distance. Given m = 24 and v = 72.0m, u = v/m = 72/24 = 3.0m. The trap here is multiplying instead of dividing (72 × 24), which would wildly overshoot any sensible slide-to-lens distance — always sanity-check that the object distance for magnified projection is smaller than the image distance, not larger.

explanation: The general wave equation is y = A sin[k(x − vt)], where k = 2π/λ = 2π/0.01 ≈ 200π rad/m and wave speed v = fλ = 550 × 0.01 = 5.5 m/s. Substituting gives y = 0.15 sin[200π(x − 5.5t)], matching option A exactly in both the wavenumber and the wave speed factored inside the bracket. The distractors scramble which numbers belong with x versus t, so always derive k and v independently before matching to the options.

explanation: This is the classic regelation demonstration: pressure from the thin wire lowers the local melting point of ice, melting it just ahead of the wire; once the wire passes, the pressure is released and the water instantly refreezes behind it, leaving the ice block intact. question_text: [Waves — Standing/Progressive Waves on Strings] One end of a long wire is fixed while a vibrator is attached to the other end. When the vibrator is energized, the types of waves generated in the wire are
options_json: ["stationary and longitudinal","stationary and transverse","progressive and transverse","progressive and longitudinal"]
explanation: The vibrator produces transverse waves (particle motion perpendicular to the wire), which travel along the wire and reflect off the fixed end. The incident and reflected waves of the same frequency and amplitude superpose to form a stationary (standing) wave pattern with fixed nodes and antinodes. This is the working principle behind sonometer and Melde's experiment setups tested regularly in JAMB.

question_text: [Modern Physics — Photoelectric Effect] Light of energy 5eV falls on a metal of work function 3eV and electrons are liberated. The stopping potential is
explanation: By Einstein's photoelectric equation, the maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons equals photon energy minus work function: KE_max = 5eV − 3eV = 2eV. Since the stopping potential (in volts) numerically equals the maximum kinetic energy (in eV) divided by the electron charge, the stopping potential is 2.0V. The trap is adding instead of subtracting the work function, which produces option D.

question_text: [Optics — Optical Instruments] What optical instrument can best be constructed with converging lenses of focal lengths 50cm and 5cm?
explanation: An astronomical (refracting) telescope uses two converging lenses: an objective of long focal length (50cm) and an eyepiece of short focal length (5cm), separated by the sum of their focal lengths for normal adjustment. A compound microscope also uses two converging lenses but both have short focal lengths for high magnification of nearby objects, which doesn't fit this 50cm/5cm pairing designed for distant objects.

explanation: Since (1/2)ⁿ = 1/64 = (1/2)⁶, exactly 6 half-lives have elapsed in 120 years, giving a half-life of 120/6 = 20 years. question_text: [Mechanics — Power, Work and Energy] If the force and the velocity on a system are each reduced simultaneously by half, the power of the system is
explanation: Power P = Fv. If both F and v are halved, the new power is (F/2)(v/2) = Fv/4, i.e., a quarter of the original. This is a direct consequence of power depending on the product of two quantities — halving two multiplied factors always divides the product by four, not by two.

subject: Physics
question_text: [Thermal Physics — Anomalous Expansion of Water] A quantity of water at 0°C is heated to about 30°C. At each degree rise in temperature, its density will
options_json: ["rise steadily","fall steadily","fall then rise","rise then fall"]
explanation: Water exhibits anomalous expansion: as it's heated from 0°C to 4°C, it actually contracts, so density rises to a maximum at 4°C; beyond 4°C, normal thermal expansion takes over and density falls steadily as temperature continues to rise toward 30°C. This anomaly (density rising then falling, not falling then rising) is why ice floats and why lakes freeze from the top down, protecting aquatic life below.

question_text: [Optics — Reflection at Plane Mirrors] An engineer intends to deviate a light ray from its path by 120° through reflection from a plane mirror. Calculate the angle of incidence
explanation: For reflection off a plane mirror, the deviation of the ray equals 180° − 2i, where i is the angle of incidence. Setting 180 − 2i = 120 gives 2i = 60, so i = 30°. A frequent trap is confusing the angle of incidence with the deviation angle itself, or halving 120° directly (giving 60°, option A) without accounting for the 180° relationship.

question_text: [Mechanics — Circular Motion] I. Its velocity is constant II. No work is done on the body III. It has constant acceleration directed away from the centre IV. The centripetal force is directed towards the centre Which combination of the above is true of a body moving with constant speed in a circular track?
options_json: ["II and IV","I and IV","II and III","I and III"]
explanation: For uniform circular motion, speed is constant but velocity is not (its direction constantly changes), so statement I is false. The centripetal force acts toward the centre (IV, true) and is always perpendicular to the velocity, meaning it does no work on the body (II, true). Statement III is false on two counts: the acceleration is centripetal (directed toward, not away from, the centre), ruling out any option pairing III with a correct answer.

question_text: [Mechanics — Resolution of Forces / Vectors] A handbag containing some load weighing 162N is carried by two students each holding the handle of the bag next to him. If each handle is pulled 60° to the vertical, find the force on each student's arm
explanation: The two tension forces, each at 60° to the vertical, must have their vertical components sum to support the full weight: 2T·cos(60°) = 162N. Since cos(60°) = 0.5, this simplifies to 2T(0.5) = T = 162N. The trap is assuming the load simply splits evenly between the two arms (giving 81N, option A), which ignores that the greater the angle from vertical, the more tension is needed per arm to support the same vertical load.

question_text: [Current Electricity — Internal Resistance and Efficiency] A cell of internal resistance 1Ω supplies current to an external resistor of 3Ω. The efficiency of the cell is
explanation: The efficiency of a cell is the fraction of total power delivered to the external (useful) resistance: efficiency = R/(R+r) = 3/(3+1) = 3/4 = 75%. This reflects that most of the e.m.f. is being used productively in the external circuit rather than wasted as heat inside the cell's own internal resistance. The trap is computing r/(R+r) instead, inverting the fraction to give 25% (option A).

question_text: [Optics — Total Internal Reflection] Total internal reflection occurs when light moves from?
option_a: a dense medium to a less dense medium
option_d: a less dense to a dense medium
options_json: ["a dense medium to a less dense medium","air to water","water to glass","a less dense to a dense medium"]
answer_text: a dense medium to a less dense medium
explanation: Total internal reflection requires light travelling from an optically denser medium into a less dense one (e.g., glass to air), and only when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle. Options B and C both describe light entering a denser medium, which can never produce total internal reflection — light bends toward the normal instead, it does not reflect entirely. This distinction (dense-to-rare, not rare-to-dense) is the single most tested TIR fact in JAMB.

question_text: [Waves — Wave Speed on a Stretched String] A transverse wave is applied to a string whose mass per unit length is 3 x 10⁻² kgm⁻¹. If the string is under a tension 12N, the speed of the propagation of the wave is
explanation: Wave speed on a stretched string is given by v = √(T/μ), where T is tension and μ is mass per unit length. Substituting: v = √(12/0.03) = √400 = 20 m/s. This formula shows why guitar and violin strings under higher tension produce faster wave propagation, and hence higher pitched notes for a given string length.

explanation: Beta particles are fast-moving electrons and therefore carry charge, so they are deflected by both magnetic and electric fields (though less than alpha particles due to their smaller mass, they deflect much further in the same field). Gamma rays and X-rays are uncharged electromagnetic radiation and are unaffected by either type of field, which is precisely how scientists distinguish charged from uncharged radioactive emissions in a deflection experiment.

question_text: [Thermal Physics — Humidity / Hygrometry] Dry Day 1 - 30°C | Day 2 - 29°C | Day 3 - 25°C Wet Day 1 - 22°C | Day 2 - 22°C | Day 3 - 21°C The readings above are for three consecutive days from a wet and dry bulb hygrometer.
