explanation: The depression (dry-bulb minus wet-bulb reading) shrinks steadily across the three days: 8°C, 7°C, then 4°C. A smaller depression means less evaporative cooling is occurring at the wet bulb, which happens when the surrounding air is already closer to saturation — so a shrinking depression signals rising relative humidity. question_text: [Mechanics — Relative Velocity] A stream is flowing at 0.75ms⁻¹ and a boat heading perpendicular for the stream landed at the opposite bank at an angle of 30° to the direct crossing path. Calculate the velocity of the boat.
explanation: The stream's velocity is the component of the resultant velocity along the bank, related to the resultant by sin(30°) = v_stream/v_resultant. Solving: v_resultant = 0.75/sin(30°) = 0.75/0.5 = 1.50 m/s. The 30° drift angle tells us how far off-course the current pushed the boat relative to its straight-across heading, which lets us reconstruct the full resultant velocity using basic trigonometry on the velocity triangle.

explanation: The force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field is F = BIL, maximised when the conductor is perpendicular to the field. Substituting: F = 0.5 × 0.8 × 2 = 0.8N. This is the fundamental equation underlying how electric motors and moving-coil galvanometers generate mechanical force from electric current.

question_text: [Mechanics — Newton's Second Law / Tension] A rope is being used to pull a mass of 10kg vertically upward. Determine the tension in the rope if, starting from rest, the mass acquires a velocity of 4ms⁻¹ in 8s [g = 10ms⁻²]
explanation: First find acceleration: a = (v−u)/t = 4/8 = 0.5 m/s². Applying Newton's second law to a mass being lifted, the rope must overcome gravity and provide the net upward acceleration: T − mg = ma, so T = m(g+a) = 10 × (10+0.5) = 105N. The trap is calculating only the net force (ma = 5N, option A) and forgetting the rope must also support the object's full weight against gravity.

question_text: [Electromagnetism — Motion of Charges in Combined Fields] If a charged ion goes through combined electric and magnetic fields, the resultant emergent velocity of the ion is
explanation: This describes a velocity selector: when the electric force (qE) and magnetic force (qvB) on the charged ion are balanced and opposite, the ion passes straight through undeflected. Setting qE = qvB and solving gives v = E/B. This principle is used in mass spectrometers to select ions of a specific velocity before further analysis, filtering out ions travelling at any other speed.

question_text: [Thermal Physics — Calorimetry / Specific Heat Capacity] A metal of mass 0.5kg is heated to 100°C and then transferred to a well-lagged calorimeter of heat capacity 80JK⁻¹ containing water of heat capacity 420JK⁻¹ at 15°C. If the final steady temperature of the mixture is 25°C, find the specific heat capacity of the metal.

So 0.5 × c × (100−25) = (420+80) × (25−15), giving c = 500/3.75 ≈ 133 J/kg/K. A frequent trap is using only the water's heat capacity and forgetting to add the calorimeter's, which shifts the answer toward option B.

explanation: A vacuum flask's double-walled, evacuated design already blocks conduction and convection (no medium to carry heat) and its silvered walls minimise radiation. question_text: [Mechanics — Friction] I. The frictional force is independent of the area of the surfaces in contact II. The frictional force depends on the nature of the surfaces in contact III. question_text: [Mechanics — Simple Harmonic Motion / Pendulum] A simple pendulum has a period of 17.0s. When the length is shortened by 1.5m, its period is 8.5s. Calculate the original length of the pendulum
explanation: Since T = 2π√(L/g), the ratio T₁/T₂ = √(L/(L−1.5)) = 17/8.5 = 2. Squaring gives 4 = L/(L−1.5), so 4L − 6 = L, and 3L = 6, giving L = 2.0m. question_text: [Optics — Curved Mirrors] The driving mirror of a car has a radius of curvature of 1m. A vehicle behind the car is 4m from the mirror. Find the image distance behind the mirror.
explanation: > A driving (rear-view) mirror is convex, with focal length f = R/2 = 0.5m (virtual, behind the mirror). Using the mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f with the real-is-positive sign convention (f = −0.5m, u = −4m), solving gives v = −4/7m, meaning the image forms 4/7m behind the mirror. Convex mirrors always form a virtual, diminished image behind the mirror regardless of object distance — this is exactly why they give drivers a wider field of view.

question_text: [Electricity — Conduction Through Gases] I. Low pressure. II. High pressure. III. High p.d. IV. Low p.d. Which combination of the above is true of the conduction of electricity through gases?

question_text: [Thermal Physics — Work Done by a Gas] A gas with initial volume of 2 x 10⁻⁶m³ is allowed to expand to six times its initial value at constant pressure of 2 x 10⁵Nm⁻². The work done is?
explanation: > For isobaric (constant pressure) expansion, work done = PΔV = P(V₂ − V₁). Here V₂ = 6 × 2×10⁻⁶ = 12×10⁻⁶m³, so ΔV = 10×10⁻⁶m³, giving W = 2×10⁵ × 10×10⁻⁶ = 2.0J. question_text: [Electromagnetism — Transformers and Eddy Currents] Energy losses through eddy currents are reduced by using

explanation: > An absolute (constant-volume gas) thermometer uses a fixed volume of gas, typically helium, because it stays gaseous down to extremely low temperatures and behaves very close to an ideal gas over a wide range, making it the most reliable reference for defining the absolute (Kelvin) temperature scale. Mercury and alcohol thermometers, by contrast, rely on liquid expansion and cannot function anywhere near absolute zero.

question_text: [Waves — Standing Waves / Harmonics] A string is fastened tightly between two walls 24cm apart. The wavelength of the second overtone is
explanation: > For a string fixed at both ends, the nth harmonic has wavelength λₙ = 2L/n. The second overtone is the third harmonic (n=3), since the first overtone is the second harmonic. So λ₃ = 2(24)/3 = 16cm. The recurring trap in overtone questions is off-by-one errors — always remember "second overtone" means the third harmonic, not literally n=2.

question_text: [Electricity — Cost of Electrical Energy] The cost of running five 60 W lamps and four 100 W lamps for 20 hours if electrical energy cost #10.00 per kwh is
explanation: > Total power = (5×60) + (4×100) = 300 + 400 = 700W = 0.7kW. Energy used over 20 hours = 0.7 × 20 = 14kWh. At ₦10.00 per kWh, total cost = 14 × 10 = ₦140.00. question_text: [Current Electricity — Cell Efficiency and Internal Resistance] A cell of internal resistance r supplies current to a 6.0Ω resistor and its efficiency is 75%. Find the value of r.
explanation: > Cell efficiency = R/(R+r), so 0.75 = 6/(6+r), giving 6+r = 8, so r = 2.0Ω. The efficiency formula directly compares the useful external resistance to the total circuit resistance, meaning a higher internal resistance always lowers the fraction of power delivered usefully — this trade-off between r and efficiency is a frequently recurring JAMB theme.

explanation: > The Sun generates energy through nuclear fusion, where hydrogen nuclei combine under immense heat and pressure to form helium, releasing vast amounts of energy per the mass-energy equivalence relation. question_text: [Current Electricity — Terminal Voltage and Internal Resistance] A resistance R is connected across the terminal of an electric cell of internal resistance 2Ω and the voltage was reduced to 3/5 of its nominal value. The value of R is
explanation: > Terminal voltage V relates to e.m.f. ε by V/ε = R/(R+r). Setting V/ε = 3/5 and r = 2Ω: R/(R+2) = 3/5, so 5R = 3R + 6, giving 2R = 6, R = 3Ω. This models how a cell's terminal voltage always drops below its rated e.m.f. once current flows through any external resistance, due to the "lost volts" across the internal resistance.

explanation: > Inserting a dielectric like glass between capacitor plates increases capacitance because C = εᵣε₀A/d, and glass has a relative permittivity (dielectric constant) εᵣ greater than 1 (the value for air/vacuum). question_text: [Mechanics — Variation of Weight on Earth's Surface] I. The earth is not spherical but elliptical in shape II. Variation in latitude and longitude III. Rotation of the earth on its axis IV. Variation in the density of the earth On which combination of the above does the weight of an object vary on the earth's surface?
options_json: ["I, II, III and IV","III and IV only","I, II and III only","I and II only"]
explanation: > Weight (mg) varies across Earth's surface because Earth's slightly ellipsoidal shape (I) means the radius — and hence g — differs by latitude, and Earth's rotation (III) creates a centrifugal effect that reduces effective weight, strongest at the equator and zero at the poles. Longitude (part of II, alongside latitude) has no bearing on g since g depends on distance from Earth's centre and rotational effects, not east-west position — but since latitude variation alone is a genuine cause, and IV (density variation, a purely local/geological effect not part of the standard three global causes) is excluded, I, II and III together form the examiner's intended answer.

question_text: [Mechanics — Conservation of Energy] A stone of mass 1kg is dropped from a height of 10m above the ground and falls freely under gravity. Its kinetic energy 5m above the ground is then equal to
option_a: its kinetic energy on the ground
options_json: ["its kinetic energy on the ground","twice its initial potential energy","its initial potential energy","half its initial potential energy"]
explanation: > By conservation of mechanical energy, total energy (KE + PE) remains constant throughout the fall. At the halfway point (5m), exactly half of the initial potential energy has converted to kinetic energy, while the other half remains as potential energy — so KE at 5m = ½(initial PE). This halfway-point symmetry is a hallmark feature of free-fall energy conversion problems.

subject: Physics
question_text: [Waves — Harmonics on a Stretched String] Find the frequencies of the first three harmonics of a piano string of length 1.5m, if the velocity of the wave on the string is 120ms⁻¹
explanation: > The fundamental frequency of a string fixed at both ends is f₁ = v/(2L) = 120/(2×1.5) = 40Hz. Successive harmonics are integer multiples of the fundamental: f₂ = 2×40 = 80Hz, and f₃ = 3×40 = 120Hz. This whole-number multiple pattern (f, 2f, 3f...) is the defining signature of harmonics on a string fixed at both ends, distinct from the odd-harmonic-only pattern seen in pipes closed at one end.

subject: Physics
question_text: [Waves — Standing Waves in Sound / Antinodes] A plane sound wave of frequency 85.5Hz and velocity 342ms⁻¹ is reflected from a vertical wall. At what distance from the wall does the wave have antinode?
explanation: > Wavelength λ = v/f = 342/85.5 = 4m. When a sound wave reflects off a rigid wall, a node (point of zero displacement) forms at the wall itself, and the nearest antinode forms at a quarter-wavelength away: d = λ/4 = 4/4 = 1m. This node-at-the-boundary condition mirrors how a closed pipe end behaves for standing sound waves.

subject: Physics
question_text: [Electrostatics/Gravitation — Comparing Fundamental Forces] The ratio of electrostatic force F_E to gravitational force F_G between two protons each of charge e and mass m, at a distance d is
explanation: > Coulomb's law gives F_E = e²/(4πε₀d²) and Newton's law of gravitation gives F_G = Gm²/d², so their ratio F_E/F_G = e²/(4πε₀Gm²) — note the distance d cancels out entirely from the ratio, which is why none of the options contain d. This ratio famously comes out enormous (~10³⁶), illustrating just how much stronger the electrostatic force is than gravity at the subatomic scale.

subject: Physics
question_text: [Electricity — Electric Field Strength] A student is at a height 4m above the ground during a thunderstorm. Given that the potential difference between the thundercloud and the ground is 10⁷V, the electric field created by the storm is
explanation: > Electric field strength between parallel-like surfaces is E = V/d = 10⁷/4 = 2.5×10⁶ NC⁻¹. This treats the cloud-to-ground gap as a simple parallel-plate-like field, a standard simplification for estimating storm field strengths in introductory physics. The trap is using the student's height in the wrong place or forgetting to divide, both of which lead to a mismatched power of ten.

subject: Physics
question_text: [Electromagnetism — Angle of Dip] What is the angle of dip at the magnetic equator?
explanation: > The angle of dip is the angle Earth's magnetic field lines make with the horizontal at a given location. At the magnetic equator, the field lines run parallel to Earth's surface (purely horizontal, with no vertical component), giving a dip angle of exactly 0°. The dip increases progressively toward the magnetic poles, reaching a maximum of 90° (field pointing straight down/up) at the poles themselves.

subject: Physics
question_text: [Modern Physics — Radiation Shielding] Which of the following metals will provide the greatest shield against ionizing radiation?
explanation: > Lead is the standard shielding material against ionising radiation (especially gamma rays and X-rays) because of its very high density and high atomic number, which maximise the probability of photon absorption/interaction per unit thickness. Aluminium, by contrast, is commonly used only to block much less penetrating alpha and some beta particles, not the more penetrating radiation types this question implies.

question_text: [Electrochemistry — Voltaic Cells] In a Daniel cell, the depolarizer, positive and negative electrodes are respectively
option_c: sulphuric acid, lead oxide and lead
options_json: ["copper sulphate, copper and zinc","manganese dioxide, carbon and zinc","sulphuric acid, lead oxide and lead","potassium hydroxide, nickel and iron"]
explanation: > In a Daniell cell, copper sulphate solution acts as the depolarizer (preventing hydrogen gas bubbles from forming at the copper electrode, which would otherwise cause polarization and reduce current), with copper as the positive electrode and zinc as the negative electrode. The other options describe entirely different cell types: manganese dioxide/carbon/zinc is a dry (Leclanché) cell, while sulphuric acid/lead oxide/lead is a lead-acid accumulator.

question_text: [Mechanics — Vector Addition of Forces] The resultant of two forces acting on an object is maximum if the angle between them is
explanation: > The resultant of two forces is given by R = √(F₁² + F₂² + 2F₁F₂cosθ), which is maximised when cosθ = 1, i.e., when θ = 0° and both forces point in exactly the same direction, so their magnitudes add directly. At 180° (opposite directions), the resultant would instead be at its minimum, which is the trap many students confuse with the maximum case.

question_text: [Electromagnetism — Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor] The force on a current carrying conductor in a magnetic field is greatest when the
option_a: conductor makes an angle of 60° with the field
option_b: force is independent of the angles between the fields and the conductor
option_c: conductor is parallel with the field
option_d: conductor is at right angle with the field
options_json: ["conductor makes an angle of 60° with the field","force is independent of the angles between the fields and the conductor","conductor is parallel with the field","conductor is at right angle with the field"]
answer_text: conductor is at right angle with the field
explanation: > The force on a current-carrying conductor is F = BIL sinθ, where θ is the angle between the conductor and the field. This is maximised when sinθ = 1, i.e., θ = 90° (conductor perpendicular to the field). When the conductor is parallel to the field (θ = 0°), sinθ = 0 and the force drops to zero entirely — this is why motors and generators are designed with coils oriented to maximise this perpendicular geometry.

question_text: [Optics — Rotation of Reflected Rays] A ray of light strikes a plane mirror at an angle of incidence of 35°. If the mirror is rotated through 10°, through what angle is the reflected ray rotated?
explanation: > A key optical law states that when a plane mirror is rotated through an angle θ (with the incident ray fixed), the reflected ray rotates through 2θ — twice the mirror's rotation — regardless of the original angle of incidence. Here, rotating the mirror by 10° rotates the reflected ray by 2×10° = 20°. The original 35° incidence angle is a distractor; it plays no role in this particular calculation.

explanation: > At resonance in a series RLC circuit, the inductive and capacitive reactances exactly cancel (X_L = X_C), leaving only resistance to oppose the current. This means voltage and current are perfectly in phase, giving a phase angle of 0°. This in-phase condition is precisely what makes resonance the point of maximum current flow in a series RLC circuit.

explanation: > Power input to the motor is P = VI = 250 × 1.5 = 375W. Power output = efficiency × power input = 0.8 × 375 = 300W. The remaining 75W (375 − 300) is lost as heat and friction within the motor itself, which is exactly what "efficiency less than 100%" always represents for real machines and motors.

option_a: c circuit is given as 2 sin wt. Determine the

explanation: > The "d.c. equivalent" of an AC current refers to its RMS (root-mean-square) value, which for a sinusoidal current i = I₀sin(ωt) is I_rms = I₀/√2. Here I₀ = 2A, so I_rms = 2/√2 = √2 A. The RMS value is defined precisely because it's the DC current that would dissipate the same average power in a resistor as the actual AC current does.

question_text: [Electricity — LC Resonance] A capacitor of 20 x 10⁻¹²F and an inductor are joined in series. The value of the inductance that will give the circuit a resonance frequency of 200 kHz is
explanation: > Resonance frequency for an LC circuit is f = 1/(2π√(LC)), so L = 1/((2πf)²C). Substituting f = 200×10³Hz and C = 20×10⁻¹²F gives L ≈ 0.0317H, which is closest to 1/32 H (≈0.03125H) among the given options. This LC resonance relationship is the basis for tuning circuits in radios, where L or C is adjusted to select a desired station's frequency.

question_text: [Thermal Physics — Gas Laws / Combined Gas Law] The pressure of a given mass of a gas changes from 300Nm⁻² to 120Nm⁻² while the temperature drops from 127°C to −73°C. The ratio of the final volume to the initial volume is
explanation: > Using the combined gas law (P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂) with temperatures converted to Kelvin (T₁ = 127+273 = 400K, T₂ = −73+273 = 200K): V₂/V₁ = (P₁T₂)/(P₂T₁) = (300×200)/(120×400) = 60000/48000 = 1.25 = 5/4. The critical step many students skip is converting Celsius to Kelvin before substituting — gas law ratios only work correctly with absolute temperature.

question_text: [Mechanics — Simple Machines / Efficiency] The efficiency of a machine is always less than 100% because the
option_a: work output is always greater than the work input
option_b: load lifted is always greater than the effort applied

This gap — VR always exceeding MA — is precisely why no real machine can reach 100% efficiency.

In the same way, we can define an even number as a finite integer divisible by two or a democracy as a system of government in which the people themselves rule.

Today, the deregulation of some of these sectors has broken its monopoly and introduced healthy competition to make a little easier for Nigerians. A good example is the breaking of the stifling monopoly of Nigeria Airways. Today, the traveller is king at the domestic airports as opposed to the struggle that air travels used to be under Nigeria Airways monopoly. Before, it was almost easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for travellers to board a plane.

In the same way, the government argues that if the current NNPC monopoly were broken with the introduction of entrepreneurs to the refining and sale of petroleum products in the country, the Nigerian people would be all the better for it. It stands to reason that once the government continues to fix maximum prices would be all the better for it. It stands to reason that once the government continues to fix maximum prices for petroleum products in this country, the deregulation of the oil sector should bring some relief to the people by ensuring that wastage, corruption and inefficiency are reduced to the minimum. option_b: the government should deregulate every aspect of the nigerian economy

option_d: competition should be allowed in the production and distribution of petroleum products

question_text:
Recgnizing the need for objectivity in their work, the early report writers to develop a writing style which convey this attitude. They reasoned that the source of the subjective quality in a report is the human being.  And they reasoned that objectivity is best attained by emphasizing the factual material of a report rather 5than the personalities involved. So they worked to remove the human being from their writing. Impersonal writing style was the result. By impersonal writing is meant writing in the third person-without I’s, we’s or you’s.

In recent years, impersonal writing has been strenuously questioned by many writers. These writers point out that personal writing is more forceful and direct than is impersonal writing. They contend that writing which brings both reader and writer into the picture is more like conversation and therefore more interesting. And the answer to the point on objectivity when written in personal style as when in impersonal style. Frequently, they counter with the argument that impersonal writing leads to an overuse of passive voice and a generally dull writing style. This last argument however lacks substances. Impersonal writing can and should be interesting. Any dullness it may have is wholly the fault of the writer. As proof, one has only to look at the lovely styles used by the writers for newspapers, news magazines and journals. Most of this writing is impersonal and usually it is not dull.

As in most cases of controversy, there is some merit to the arguments on both sides. There are situations in which personal writing is best. There are situations in which impersonal writing is best. And there are situations in which either style is appropriate. The writer must decide at the outset of his work which style is best for his own situation.

Her decision should be based on the circumstances of each report situation. First, he should consider the expectations or desires of those for whom he is preparing the report. More than likely he will find a preference for impersonal style for like most human beings; businessman has been slow to break tradition. Next, the writer should consider the formality of the report situation. If the situation is informal, as when the report is really a personal communication of information between business associates, personal writing is appropriate. But if the situation is formal, as is case with most reports, the conventional impersonal style is best.

option_a: is more forceful and direct than impersonal writing
option_b: can be more objective than impersonal writing
option_c: is the style to use in all situations involving businessmen
option_d: has informal features which make it more diverting than impersonal writing

answer_text: is more forceful and direct than impersonal writing
explanation: The passage explicitly states this argument: 'personal writing is more forceful and direct than is impersonal writing.'

question_text:
Recgnizing the need for objectivity in their work, the early report writers to develop a writing style which convey this attitude. They reasoned that the source of the subjective quality in a report is the human being.  And they reasoned that objectivity is best attained by emphasizing the factual material of a report rather 5than the personalities involved. So they worked to remove the human being from their writing. Impersonal writing style was the result. By impersonal writing is meant writing in the third person-without I’s, we’s or you’s.

In recent years, impersonal writing has been strenuously questioned by many writers. These writers point out that personal writing is more forceful and direct than is impersonal writing. They contend that writing which brings both reader and writer into the picture is more like conversation and therefore more interesting. And the answer to the point on objectivity when written in personal style as when in impersonal style. If our thoughts is to be clear and we are to succeed in communicating it to other people, we must have some method of fixing the meaning of the words we use. When we use a word whose meaning is not certain, we may well be asked to define it. There is a usual traditional device for doing this by indicating the class to which whatever is indicated by the term belongs and also other particular property which distinguishes it from all other members of the same class. They contend that writing which brings both reader and writer into the picture is more like conversation and therefore more interesting. And the answer to the point on objectivity when written in personal style as when in impersonal style. Frequently, they counter with the argument that impersonal writing leads to an overuse of passive voice and a generally dull writing style. This last argument however lacks substances. Impersonal writing can and should be interesting. Any dullness it may have is wholly the fault of the writer. As proof, one has only to look at the lovely styles used by the writers for newspapers, news magazines and journals. Most of this writing is impersonal and usually it is not dull.

As in most cases of controversy, there is some merit to the arguments on both sides. There are situations in which personal writing is best. There are situations in which impersonal writing is best. And there are situations in which either style is appropriate. The writer must decide at the outset of his work which style is best for his own situation.

Next, the writer should consider the formality of the report situation. If the situation is informal, as when the report is really a personal communication of information between business associates, personal writing is appropriate.
